item.title: Addictive behaviors involving digital technologies
item.content:encoded:
This special issue examines addictive behaviors associated with digital technologies, addressing emerging public health concerns related to excessive and problematic use of internet platforms, gaming, and social media. The collection seeks to advance understanding of how digital technologies can foster addictive patterns of behavior and their implications for individual and population health.

Appel publié par Public Health. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Digital technology addiction
  • Problematic internet use
  • Gaming addiction
  • Social media addiction
  • Behavioral addictions

Timeline

  • September 1, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Advancing Food Quality and Sustainable Food Systems through Post-Harvest Innovations, Cold Chains, and Digital Technologies
item.content:encoded:
Harshad Sonar, Indian Institute of Management (IIM)

Bishal Dey Sarkar, Indian Institute of Management (IIM)

Joash Mageto, University of Johannesburg

Samuel Fosso Wamba, TBS Education

This special issue addresses how post-harvest innovations, cold-chain operations, and digital technologies can enhance food quality and sustainability across supply chains. The editors recognize that food losses stem from interconnected operational and infrastructural challenges, particularly in developing economies. The call seeks integrated research that connects previously separate topics to understand how innovations work together to improve food system outcomes.

The issue welcomes interdisciplinary contributions examining how post-harvest innovations, cold-chain strategies, digital technologies like AI and blockchain, and collaborative governance can reduce waste, improve transparency, and build resilient food systems. Research should prioritize food-centric outcomes and provide actionable insights for researchers, policymakers, producers, and stakeholders developing safer and more sustainable food systems.

Appel publié par British Food Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Post-harvest management for food quality preservation and food loss reduction
  • Cold chain management for food safety, nutritional quality, and perishability
  • Digital technologies for food quality, traceability, and transparency
  • Smart packaging and innovative food preservation technologies
  • Sustainable and resilient food systems under climate and supply chain disruptions
  • Food waste reduction, circular food systems, and resource-efficient post-harvest practices
  • Food safety governance, regulatory compliance, and stakeholder collaboration
  • Data-driven decision making and policy innovations for sustainable food security

Timeline

  • January 9, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • February 28, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Consumption trends of Cultural and Creative products in "phygital" contexts
item.content:encoded:
Elisa Salvador, ESSCA School of Management

Carmen Pérez-Cabañero, Universitat de Valencia

This special issue examines how consumption of cultural and creative products is evolving in contemporary "phygital" contexts where digital and physical experiences merge. The call seeks papers addressing contemporary theories of consumer behaviour, novel methodologies, and factors spanning economic, psychological, social, and technological dimensions that shape how people engage with cultural offerings.

The issue aims to map current consumption trends at individual and societal levels, identify best practices, and address gaps in academic understanding of how cultural industries are adapting to rapid societal transformation. It focuses on ten cultural domains including heritage, archives, libraries, publishing, visual arts, performing arts, audiovisual media, architecture, advertising, and crafts.

The special issue recognizes that cultural and creative industries are responding to challenges through innovation in digital environments, extended reality technologies, and sustainable practices. Papers should explore how these emerging practices contribute to individual wellbeing and broader social benefits such as education, intercultural dialogue, and social cohesion.

Appel publié par Arts and the Market. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Cultural and Creative Industries (CCIs) consumption patterns in phygital environments
  • Consumer behaviour theories and frameworks related to cultural products and services
  • Qualitative and quantitative methodologies for studying cultural consumption
  • Economic, psychological, social, and technological factors influencing purchasing decisions for cultural goods
  • Case studies of consumption trends across different geographic and cultural contexts
  • Phygital experiences integrating digital and physical elements in cultural settings
  • Role of artificial intelligence and extended reality technologies (augmented reality, virtual reality) in cultural consumption
  • Sustainability and circular practices in CCIs
  • Impact of CCIs on regional development, economic growth, cultural innovation, and social cohesion
  • Memorability and wellbeing benefits of phygital cultural experiences

  • July 15, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • February 15, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Relational pedagogies in an age of GenAI
item.content:encoded:
Karen Gravett, University of Surrey

Naomi Winstone, University of Surrey

Kieran Balloo, Southern Cross University

This special issue explores relational pedagogies—teaching practices emphasizing meaningful connections between teachers and students, and engagement with both human and nonhuman entities like digital technologies—within contemporary higher education contexts shaped by generative artificial intelligence. Relational pedagogies foster emotional and affective dimensions of education while challenging competitive individualistic approaches.

The rapid emergence of GenAI is fundamentally reshaping how educators and students interact, redefining educational practices politically, practically, and ideologically. The special issue seeks critical perspectives on how GenAI reconfigures relationality in higher education, addressing questions about student engagement with AI outside educator control, evolving assessment and feedback practices, care in digitalized contexts, equity implications, and the ethical and environmental concerns these technologies raise.

Appel publié par Teaching in Higher Education. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Discourses surrounding GenAI and pedagogy
  • Relationality with respect to assessment practices
  • Relational feedback processes
  • The role of care and its connection with GenAI in contemporary universities
  • The intersection of AI technologies with notions of mattering and belonging
  • Research into academic work and relational connections
  • The materiality of education
  • Political and ethical questions regarding digital technologies such as surveillance, datafication, and agency
  • GenAI's environmental impacts and their intersection with pedagogical, ethical, and political questions
  • Posthuman, sociomaterial and feminist materialist perspectives
  • How does students' use of GenAI reshape relationships and pedagogies?
  • What role do emotions, affective relations, and embodied experiences play for students and educators in an age of GenAI?
  • How do relational pedagogic encounters with GenAI blur the boundaries between human and machine?
  • How are GenAI technologies changing relational assessment practices in higher education?
  • How are relational feedback processes evolving as a result of GenAI technologies?
  • What new methods are needed to understand our relationship with digital and GenAI technologies in higher education?
  • What questions does GenAI raise for equity perspectives on relationality?
  • What new theoretical and critical approaches are being engaged to investigate relational pedagogies and relationality in the age of GenAI?

item.title: Digital Technologies for Combating Unethical Labour Practices and Promoting Human Rights
item.content:encoded:
Stefan Gold, Technical University of Munich

Antoine Harfouche, Paris Nanterre University

Paul Jones, Swansea University

Maryam Lotfi, Cardiff University

Guoqing Zhao, Swansea University

Unethical labour practices affecting approximately 50 million people worldwide remain a critical social challenge. Digital technologies such as blockchain, artificial intelligence, and cloud computing offer potential solutions, yet research on their practical deployment remains limited. This special issue seeks contributions examining how these technologies can be leveraged for monitoring, detecting, reporting, and remediating unethical labour practices.

The call invites original, theory-driven research using various methodologies that provide nuanced insights into digital technology applications for addressing modern slavery, human trafficking, forced labour, and other severe labour practices. Priority is given to studies that challenge existing paradigms, explore underexamined dimensions, or offer innovative frameworks that yield both conceptual advances and practical implications for policymakers and practitioners.

Appel publié par Information Systems Frontiers. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Blockchain technology for labour monitoring
  • Artificial intelligence for detecting trafficking and slavery
  • Internet of Things and labour practices

  • Cloud computing applications
  • Worker voice technologies
  • Biometric recognition systems
  • Satellite imagery for labour monitoring
  • Machine learning for identifying at-risk populations
  • Digital technologies for survivor support and reintegration
  • Supply chain transparency and digital tracking
  • Modern slavery detection and prevention
  • Child labour monitoring
  • Forced labour identification
  • Human trafficking detection
  • Bonded labour practices
  • Digital solutions for labour compliance
  • Technology adoption in human rights

item.title: Unpacking Digitalization: Antecedents, Strategies, and Performance Implications
item.content:encoded:
Jasmina Berbegal-Mirabent, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya

Angelo Cavallo, Politecnico di Milano

Antje Fiedler, University of Auckland

Esteban Lafuente, Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica

Digital transformation has become essential for both private and public organizations seeking innovation and competitive advantage. However, the literature lacks coherent understanding of how digitalization is implemented across different contexts. While large organizations traditionally led these efforts, SMEs and public institutions increasingly must engage in digital transformation despite significant resource constraints.

The relationship between digitalization and performance is complex and context-dependent. Digital technologies offer opportunities for innovation and efficiency but also carry risks of misalignment with strategy and organizational disruption. Success requires aligning digital initiatives with organizational capabilities, workforce skills, and strategic planning rather than technology adoption alone.

This special issue seeks contributions examining how organizations manage digitalization efforts across private firms and public institutions, addressing the drivers of digital transformation, mechanisms through which digitalization influences performance outcomes, and how digital transformation reshapes competitive dynamics in different economic contexts.

Appel publié par Review of Managerial Science. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Theorising Time in a Digital Era: New Horizons for IS Research
item.content:encoded:
Kieran Conboy, University of Galway

Sirkka L. Jarvenpaa, The University of Texas at Austin

Brian T. Pentland, Michigan State University

Efpraxia D. Zamani, Durham University

Digital technologies have fundamentally transformed how we experience time and temporality, influencing work, life, and identity through accelerated communication and constant connectivity. While temporality—encompassing speed, duration, sequencing, rhythm, and timing—is central to how information systems are designed and studied, IS research has largely treated it simplistically, focusing narrowly on clock-time, speed, and duration rather than engaging with its complex, multifaceted nature.

The field lacks cumulative theoretical development on time despite growing recognition of its importance. IS researchers quickly highlight technology's impact on organisational speed but are slow to address temporal complexity comprehensively. Time remains theoretically elusive, often excluded or treated as a hidden dimension in contemporary IS studies. This special issue seeks to advance theoretical understanding of how temporal dynamics influence IS phenomena across multiple scales, from micro-temporal moment-to-moment interactions to macro-temporal institutional transformations.

Appel publié par European Journal of Information Systems. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How digital interfaces, notifications, and data streams reconfigure everyday temporal experience, including attention, interruption, multitasking, and asynchronous collaboration
  • How people make sense of their digital pasts through data archives or online traces, and how they anticipate algorithmic or digitally mediated futures
  • How workflow systems, dashboards, collaboration platforms, enterprise analytics, and predictive tools recalibrate shared temporal expectations and influence coordination
  • How temporal orientations embedded in tools or analytics shape decision processes, innovation, or strategic flexibility
  • Temporal properties of digital artefacts including update cycles, data retention logics, algorithmic refresh rates, and security time horizons
  • How data governance, privacy regimes, or AI systems handle conflicting temporal demands
  • Why certain digital transformations accelerate rapidly while others evolve slowly and unevenly
  • How digital standards, platforms, and protocols sediment, diffuse, or become institutionalised over time
  • How temporal imaginaries, time horizons, or long-term digital trajectories shape fields, industries, and societies
  • Theoretical and methodological discussions of time in IS research, including flows, sequences, rhythms, tempos, trajectories, paths, and path nets
  • How IS research can theorise and design for extended temporal horizons to address grand challenges like climate change, pandemics, inequality, and social movements
  • How temporal assumptions are embedded in IS through algorithmic schedules, design methods like agile and continuous development, and real-time vs. asynchronous communication
  • How such temporal assumptions align or collide with individual or cultural constructions of time
  • Methodological approaches for studying temporal complexity, including computational techniques and trace data analysis
